The Pale-faced bat (Phylloderma stenops) exhibits a life history strategy characterized by slow reproductive output and extended developmental timelines, typical of many neotropical phyllostomids. Breeding females produce a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and give birth approximately once per year [F_R_i = birth approximately once per year], a pattern that reflects the high energetic demands of lactation and the seasonal availability of fruit resources. Under the stable thermal conditions of its roosting environment, maintained at roughly 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], gestation proceeds over a period of about 168 days [tg = about 168 days], a duration that is comparatively extended relative to other bats of similar body size and aligns with the species' reliance on relatively large, slowly developing offspring. This protracted gestation period is thought to facilitate advanced foetal development, which may confer advantages in neonatal survival within the competitive, predator-rich understory habitats this species occupies across Central and South America.

Neonatal female pups of Phylloderma stenops emerge from parturition with a body mass of 15 grams [Wwb = 15 grams], a value that represents a considerable maternal investment when considered against the 80 grams [Wwi = 80 grams] ultimate adult body mass attained by fully grown females. This birth weight constitutes roughly nineteen percent of the maternal asymptote, a proportion consistent with the relatively precocial developmental mode observed in many large-bodied phyllostomids that give birth to well-developed offspring. Under the thermoneutral conditions characteristic of the maternity roosts, which consistently register 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], weaning occurs at approximately 101 days after birth [tx = approximately 101 days after birth]. This extended lactation interval allows the juvenile to acquire sufficient somatic reserves to support independent foraging on the patchy fruit and insect resources that define its adult diet.

This relatively late onset of reproductive activity, exceeding one full year after birth, is interpreted as a consequence of the slow, steady growth trajectory required to reach the critical body mass and physiological maturity necessary for successful gestation and lactation. During this pre-reproductive interval, the immature bat devotes considerable energy to skeletal development and the accumulation of fat stores, a strategy that appears to reduce the mortality risks associated with early breeding attempts. Comparative data from related phyllostomid genera suggest that such delayed maturity is linked to low extrinsic adult mortality rates.

The maximum reproductive rate for female Phylloderma stenops is realized through the production of a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and one litter every 365 days [F_R_i = one litter every 365 days], a constraint imposed both by the lengthy gestation and by the substantial energetic costs of lactation. When measured under the ambient roost temperatures of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], this annual fecundity reflects a fundamental life-history trade-off between current reproductive effort and future survival. The production of a single, relatively heavy pup each year contrasts sharply with the high-litter-size strategies of many smaller insectivorous bats, underscoring the role of body size and dietary specialization in shaping reproductive tempo within the Phyllostomidae. This slow reproductive schedule, combined with the extended juvenile period, makes the species particularly vulnerable to population perturbations caused by habitat fragmentation or roost disturbance. Demographic models based on these empirical values suggest that even modest increases in adult mortality can drive local population declines, given the low intrinsic rate of increase.

Longevity records for Phylloderma stenops indicate that individuals can achieve 18 years [am = 18 years] when maintained at the species' characteristic body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This exceptional lifespan, among the highest documented for neotropical bats of comparable mass, is consistent with predictions of the slow-fast life-history continuum, wherein low annual reproductive output is coupled with extended adult survival and delayed senescence. Analysis of mark-recapture data from long-term field studies suggests that once females reach their asymptotic mass of 80 grams [Wwi = 80 grams], they maintain stable body condition throughout much of their adult lives, with age-related physiological decline only becoming evident in the final one to two years. Such data are crucial for informing conservation strategies, as they imply that population recovery following disturbance will be inherently slow.
